sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the colors, shapes, and directions of the piece carry the mood its message calls for? No.** The copy promises a cheerful day out: "All aboard", free rides, "bring a hat and a thermos". The design looks like a corporate notice. It uses only charcoal (#1f2125 or so) and grey on flat white, with no colour that suggests water, sky, or morning. The headline (roughly x 90–835, y 150–355) is set in heavy caps with negative tracking, so it reads as shouting rather than inviting. Everything sits in one static block hugging the left edge. The right half (x ≈ 840–1280) and the bottom 40% (y ≈ 470–800) are empty, and nothing gives the sense of movement or departure that a ferry headline calls for. A viewer gets the facts but not the pull to come along. On colour, Itten (*The Art of Color*) ties colour temperature and value to the emotion a piece carries. The shape and direction part has no approved source here, so treat it as my taste. Direction of fix: bring in one warm or sea-and-sky colour with a job, such as the headline or a field behind it. Then give the composition a sense of going somewhere, for example with the headline running across the full width or a horizontal band or wave that uses the empty right and lower areas. Keep the type. **Convention (colour, Itten); taste (shape and direction).** Weight: **major**. This is a promotional piece, and its job is to make people want to come.

2. **Copy gap (not a checklist line, from "the words are part of the design").** The piece names an event ("City Harbour Open Day") but gives no date, no start or end time, and no location beyond "the north landing". "Every half hour" has no starting point. A stranger cannot act on it: they don't know which day to turn up, when the first ferry leaves, or which harbour's north landing is meant. Dates and times are exactly what viewers act on, so this is a defect. Direction of fix: add the date and the hours of the rides, for example "Saturday 14 June, every half hour from 9 am to 4 pm", and make the landing findable. If this is a hero banner with the details further down the page, say so and it becomes minor. **Defect.** Weight: **major**.

**What's working.**
- **Reduction.** There are three text elements and nothing decorative, so the message (free ferry rides at the open day) is clear in one sentence within a second.
- **One voice.** A single grotesque in one ink colour gives one coherent mood and era, so nothing reads as pasted in from elsewhere.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (colours, shapes, and directions carry the mood).

**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands at once on the huge black condensed headline "ALL ABOARD THE MORNING FERRY" (about x 90–830, y 150–350). It then drops to the body line at y 405–460, and only after that goes back up to the small grey eyebrow at y 100. It reads as a poster or landing hero for a public harbour event. It feels bold and plain, and the right half and lower third are empty. Job (assumed): tell passers-by about a free ferry ride at an open day so they turn up.

What matters first:
- One element dominates: **yes**. The headline is roughly 5–6× the body size and the darkest mass on the page.
- Distinct text levels, no near-equal sizes: **yes**. There are three sizes: eyebrow about 14 px in bold grey caps, headline about 110 px, body about 20 px in regular weight. The eyebrow and body differ in size, case, weight and colour.
- Headings differ by more than size: **yes**. The headline is heavy black against regular-weight body text.

No line answered `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The headline takes over completely.** At about 110 px heavy black against about 20 px regular body text, there is no doubt where to start. The size and weight jump is big enough that it reads as a choice, not a drift (Bringhurst, a scale with real steps).
- **The three levels each have one job and look different from each other.** The eyebrow (small, bold, grey caps), the headline (huge, heavy, near-black) and the body (medium, regular, sentence case) use size, case, weight and colour together. No two can be confused, even at a glance.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the content sits in the top-left block, from x≈90 to 830 and y≈90 to 460. The headline is near-black and huge, so it is the heaviest thing on the page by far. Nothing on the right (x 830–1280) or the bottom (y 460–800) answers it. That is about 340 px of empty space below the last line of body text, roughly 40% of the frame's height. The page looks like it's tipping up and to the left. The viewer finishes "hat and a thermos." and the page just stops, so it looks unfinished, like a hero section whose content never loaded or a poster with its lower half cut off. Rule: Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": weight comes from size, darkness and isolation, and a heavy side needs a counterweight. There are two ways to fix it. Either put something in the lower or right area that earns its place (an event announcement most needs a date, times and a place, so a strong block of the open-day details would do it), or scale and place the existing block so it uses the whole frame. The empty space itself can stay as a deliberate open area; it just needs something set against it. Convention (Arnheim). Weight: major, because the unfinished look decides whether this reads as a designed poster or a page that broke.

**What's working.**
- **One strict left edge.** The eyebrow, both headline lines and the body all start at x≈90, so the block reads as one firm column with no near-misses. Keep that edge when you add anything.
- **Tight, single grouping.** The eyebrow, headline and body are spaced about the same (~45 px and ~55 px gaps), so the block reads as one unit and the eye runs straight from label to headline to body with nothing pulling it away.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Are strings of capitals and small capitals letterspaced?** No. The all-caps headline "ALL ABOARD THE / MORNING FERRY" (about x 90–835, y 150–350) has strongly negative tracking. Letters touch or merge: the two Ls in "ALL", the "RD" in "ABOARD", the "NIN" in "MORNING", and the "ERR" in "FERRY". The word spaces have almost closed, so at a glance it reads "ALLABOARD THE / MORNINGFERRY". Each line turns into one dark bar, and the viewer has to work out where words end and letters begin, in the one line that has to land at a glance. The eyebrow "CITY HARBOUR OPEN DAY" at (90, 100) has the same problem at small size: the caps are tightened rather than opened, so "HARBOUROPENDAY" runs together and the small grey label is harder to read than it needs to be. Why: Bringhurst (*Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.1.6, p. 30) says strings of capitals are letterspaced, normally 5–10% of the type size. Hochuli (*Detail in Typography*, p. 30) says "individual letters should not touch". Lupton (*Thinking with Type*, p. 81) calls negative tracking "rarely desirable" and says to use it sparingly. Large display caps can take some tightening, but not to the point where letters collide and word spaces disappear. Fix: open the headline tracking until no letters touch and every word space reads clearly. It can still be a little tight for poster punch. Give the eyebrow positive tracking of about 5–10% so its three words separate. Defect for the headline (words fuse and letters collide); convention for the eyebrow. Weight: major. The headline is the focal point and the main message, and fixing it noticeably changes how fast and cleanly it reads.

**What's working.**
- The body paragraph "Free rides every half hour from the north landing. Bring a hat and a thermos." is set at a comfortable size (about 20 px) in plain sentence case, with lines of about 60 characters and generous leading. It reads in one easy pass, and the last line is not a lone word.
- The headline breaks at the phrase boundary ("ALL ABOARD THE / MORNING FERRY") and its two lines are set tight enough to read as one unit. That gives the poster scale a clean shape once the tracking is fixed.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the headline is live text or a picture of text, which matters if this is a web page (WCAG 1.4.5). Check in the page source.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 1 no (strings of capitals letterspaced), 1 unsure (text is real type rather than a picture of text)

Walk (working notes): Bash was refused, so I couldn't run the crop script and worked from the whole image (about 1280×800, one screen). First read: the eye lands on the huge near-black headline, drops to the body line, and only then picks up the small gray eyebrow. It reads as a plain, typographic event announcement. Color: small palette yes · saturated color kept small yes · value range yes · warm/cool yes (no hue) · matching colors consistent yes · no vibrating edges yes · status colors yes (none) · color not sole carrier yes · dark-theme gray yes (light theme). Since nothing came out `no` or `unsure`, there were no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is almost entirely neutral: white ground, near-black type and one cool gray. There's no hue at all.

**Findings**
None.

(Not a checklist failure, but the director may want it: the piece is for a harbour open day, and with no hue anywhere it reads cool and corporate rather than outdoors and festive. One accent, such as a sea or sunrise hue on the eyebrow or one headline word, would give it a mood. This is taste, and minor.)

**What's working.**
- **Clear light and dark.** The near-black headline (about 90–355 y) on white is the strongest value contrast on the page. In grayscale the order is unchanged: headline, then body, then eyebrow. Value alone carries the hierarchy.
- **Few colors, used consistently.** There's one dark for the headline and body and one muted blue-gray for the eyebrow (about 90,100). The gray marks the eyebrow as a label without competing with the headline, so nothing in color pulls against the type.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

The image has no pictures, so I stopped after step 1, as the instructions say to do for a section that doesn't apply.

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image (1280×800) holds only type: an eyebrow line, a two-line display headline and a two-line body paragraph. It has no photo, illustration, icon, logo or mark.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The right side of the frame (about x 840–1280) and everything below the body text (about y 470–800) are empty. A hero layout like this one often puts a picture in that space, so a ferry or harbour image may have failed to load or not loaded yet when the screenshot was taken. I can't see a broken-image icon or a placeholder box, so this is not a finding. To check, load the live page and see whether an image request fails or is lazy-loaded into that area. If the space is meant to be empty, it belongs to the arrangement critic, not this section.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
